fetched_contents.text: Demystifying Bag of Words and TF-IDF: Foundations of Text Representation in NLP | by Ranjeet Singh (Test Automation & DevOps Engineer) In the ever-evolving world of Natural Language Processing (NLP), one of the foundational challenges is how to represent text data in a way that algorithms can understand. Before diving into the deep waters of transformers and large language models, it’s essential to grasp the basics of text vectorization. Two of the most fundamental techniques in this space are Bag of Words (BoW) and TF-IDF (Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency). In this blog, we’ll explore: * What is Bag of Words? * Limitations of BoW * What is TF-IDF? * Mathematical intuition behind TF-IDF * Python implementation using scikit-learn * When to use BoW vs. TF-IDF What is Bag of Words? The Bag of Words model is a simple and intuitive method to convert text into numerical feature vectors. It treats a document as a “bag” (multiset) of its words, disregarding grammar and word order but keeping multiplicity. How it works: 1. Vocabulary Creation: Collect all unique words from the corpus. 2. Vectorization: For each document, count the number of times each word appears. 3. Representation: Each document becomes a vector of word counts. Example Step 1: Sample Text Let’s say we have two short sentences (documents): Doc1: "The cat sat on the mat" Doc2: "The dog sat on the log" Step 2: Build the Vocabulary We list all unique words across both sentences: | Vocabulary | | | | | | | | ---------- | --- | --- | -- | --- | --- | --- | | the | cat | sat | on | mat | dog | log | So the vocabulary size = 7. Step 3: Create Vectors (Word Counts) Now we count how many times each word appears in each document. | Word | Doc1 | Doc2 | | ---- | ---- | ---- | | the | 2 | 2 | | cat | 1 | 0 | | sat | 1 | 1 | | on | 1 | 1 | | mat | 1 | 0 | | dog | 0 | 1 | | log | 0 | 1 | Step 4: Represent Each Document as a Vector * Doc1 → [2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0] * Doc2 → [2, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1] Final Bag of Words Representation Each position corresponds to one word in the vocabulary. | Document | Vector Representation | | -------- | --------------------- | | Doc1 | [2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0] | | Doc2 | [2, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1] | Limitations of Bag of Words While BoW is easy to implement and often effective, it has some drawbacks: * Ignores word order: “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” are treated the same. * Sparse vectors: Large vocabularies lead to high-dimensional, sparse vectors. * No semantic understanding: Synonyms and context are lost. To address these issues, we turn to a more refined technique: TF-IDF. What is TF-IDF? TF-IDF stands for Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency. It improves upon BoW by not just counting word occurrences, but also considering how important a word is to a document in the context of the entire corpus. Intuition: * Words like “the”, “is”, and “and” appear frequently across all documents but carry little unique information. * TF-IDF down-weights such common words and upweights rare but informative ones. The first generation of semantic space models is the vector space model for information retrieval.[15][16][17] Such vector space models for words and their distributional data implemented in their simplest form results in a very sparse vector space of high dimensionality (cf. curse of dimensionality). Reducing the number of dimensions using linear algebraic methods such as singular value decomposition then led to the introduction of latent semantic analysis in the late 1980s and the random indexing approach for collecting word co-occurrence contexts.[18][19][20][21] In 2000, Bengio et al. provided in a series of papers titled "Neural probabilistic language models" to reduce the high dimensionality of word representations in contexts by "learning a distributed representation for words".[22][23][24] A study published in NeurIPS (NIPS) 2002 introduced the use of both word and document embeddings applying the method of kernel CCA to bilingual (and multi-lingual) corpora, also providing an early example of self-supervised learning of word embeddings.[25] Word embeddings come in two different styles, one in which words are expressed as vectors of co-occurring words, and another in which words are expressed as vectors of linguistic contexts in which the words occur; these different styles are studied in Lavelli et al., 2004.[26] Roweis and Saul published in Science how to use "locally linear embedding" (LLE) to discover representations of high dimensional data structures.[27] Most new word embedding techniques after about 2005 rely on a neural network architecture instead of more probabilistic and algebraic models, after foundational work done by Yoshua Bengio[28] and colleagues.[29][30] The approach has been adopted by many research groups after theoretical advances in 2010 had been made on the quality of vectors and the training speed of the model, as well as after hardware advances allowed for a broader parameter space to be explored profitably. fetched_contents.text: Distributed Representations Definition Understanding Distributed Representations Distributed representations are a fundamental concept in the field of machine learning and natural language processing (NLP). They refer to a way of representing data, typically words or phrases, as continuous vectors in a high-dimensional space. Unlike local representations, where each entity is represented by a unique identifier in an isolated manner (such as one-hot encoding), distributed representations capture a notion of similarity and semantic meaning by allowing an entity to be represented by a pattern of values across many dimensions. The Basics of Distributed Representations In distributed representations, also known as embeddings, the idea is that the "meaning" or "semantic content" of a data point is distributed across multiple dimensions. For example, in NLP, words with similar meanings are mapped to points in the vector space that are close to each other. This closeness is not arbitrary but is learned from the context in which words appear. This context-dependent learning is often achieved through neural network models, such as Word2Vec or GloVe, which process large corpora of text to learn these representations. One of the key advantages of distributed representations is their ability to capture fine-grained semantic relationships. For instance, in a well-trained word embedding space, synonyms would be represented by vectors that are close together, and it's even possible to perform arithmetic operations with these vectors that correspond to meaningful semantic operations (e.g., "king" - "man" + "woman" might result in a vector close to "queen"). Applications of Distributed Representations Distributed representations have a wide range of applications, particularly in tasks that involve natural language understanding. They are used for: * Word Similarity: Measuring the semantic similarity between words. * Text Classification: Categorizing documents into predefined classes. * Machine Translation: Translating text from one language to another. * Information Retrieval: Finding relevant documents in response to a query. * Sentiment Analysis: Determining the sentiment expressed in a piece of text. Moreover, distributed representations are not limited to text data. They can also be applied to other types of data, such as images, where deep learning models learn to represent images as high-dimensional vectors that capture visual features and semantics. Learning Distributed Representations Learning distributed representations typically involves training a model on a task that forces it to capture semantic or feature similarities. For text, this might involve predicting a word given its surrounding words (continuous bag of words model) or predicting surrounding words given a word (skip-gram model). During this process, the model learns to place semantically similar words closer together in the vector space. For images, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) learn distributed representations by being trained to recognize objects within images. Through layers of convolutions and pooling operations, CNNs learn to represent images in a way that captures hierarchical visual features. Challenges with Distributed Representations Despite their effectiveness, distributed representations come with their own set of challenges. One major issue is the requirement of large amounts of data to learn meaningful representations. Without sufficient data, the embeddings may not capture the true semantic relationships. Additionally, distributed representations can be computationally expensive to learn, requiring significant processing power and memory, especially for large datasets. Another challenge is the interpretability of these representations. Unlike local representations, where each dimension corresponds to a specific feature, the dimensions in distributed representations do not have an easily interpretable meaning. This can make it difficult to understand what the model has learned and to diagnose issues when the model makes incorrect predictions. Conclusion Distributed representations have revolutionized the way we approach machine learning problems, especially in the domain of NLP. By providing a way to capture the semantic similarities between entities, they enable more nuanced and sophisticated models that can tackle complex tasks. As research in this area continues to grow, we can expect to see even more innovative applications and improvements to the methods used to learn these representations.

These representations also struggled with synonymy, polysemy, and context: bag-of-words loses synonymy by counting word occurrences without considering meaning, and static embeddings conflate words with multiple meanings into a single vector, so polysemy and homonymy are not handled properly [N1-F1][N3-F3].

### 1) Why embeddings solve the problem of inefficient comparison and generalization

The main reason embeddings overcome the inefficiency of high-dimensional representations is that they use dense, lower-dimensional vectors rather than sparse, high-dimensional ones [N6-R2]. The evidence on embeddings explicitly states that they improve downstream task performance by converting high-dimensional, sparse data into dense, lower-dimensional representations [N6-R2]. This matters because dense vectors are easier to store, compare, and generalize from, especially when vocabularies are large. Earlier sparse representations, by contrast, required large vectors and were inefficient for comparison and generalization because the vectors were not compact and the computational burden increased with vocabulary size [N2-R3][N1-F1]. By reducing dimensionality while preserving meaningful relationships, embeddings make NLP models more scalable and practical.

### 2) How embeddings capture semantic similarity and analogy

Embeddings address the failure of sparse representations to encode semantic relationships by placing semantically related words close together in vector space. The distributed-representations article explains that distributed representations capture similarity and semantic meaning by allowing entities to be represented by patterns across many dimensions, so words with similar meanings are mapped to points that are close together [N4-F4]. It also says that synonyms are represented by vectors that are close together and that arithmetic operations on vectors can correspond to meaningful semantic operations, such as “king” - “man” + “woman” producing a vector close to “queen” [N4-F4]. The Wikipedia excerpt on word embeddings similarly states that word embeddings are real-valued vectors encoding meaning so that words closer in space are expected to be similar in meaning [N3-F3]. This directly solves the problem of synonymy and semantic relationships, which earlier sparse representations failed to capture [N1-F1][N2-R4].

### 3) How embeddings capture context through word co-occurrence and training objectives

Embeddings also overcome the limitation of earlier representations by capturing context through word co-occurrence and training objectives that learn from surrounding language. The distributed-representations article states that distributed representations are learned from the context in which words appear, and that models such as Word2vec or GloVe learn these representations by processing large corpora [N4-F4]. The Wikipedia overview notes that word embeddings can be obtained using language modeling and feature learning techniques, and that methods include neural networks, dimensionality reduction on the word co-occurrence matrix, probabilistic models, and explicit representation based on context [N3-F3]. It also explains the distributional hypothesis that “a word is characterized by the company it keeps,” which is the foundational idea behind co-occurrence-based training [N3-F3]. This means embeddings are not static symbol tables; they are learned representations that adapt to the statistical structure of the language and the surrounding context.

### 4) How embeddings improve downstream NLP tasks

The practical benefit of embeddings is that they improve downstream NLP tasks by providing richer and more useful representations for modeling. The Milvus article says embeddings improve downstream task performance by converting high-dimensional, sparse data into dense, lower-dimensional representations [N6-R2]. The MDPI review states that word embeddings have been shown to boost performance in NLP tasks such as syntactic parsing and sentiment analysis [N5-R3]. The comprehensive guide to word embeddings similarly notes that word embeddings are fundamental in NLP and that they capture semantic and syntactic information [N5-R2]. Taken together, this evidence shows that embeddings improve downstream tasks not just by reducing dimensionality, but by preserving and encoding meaning, context, and relationships that earlier representations lost [N6-R2][N5-R3][N5-R2].

### 5) Broader implications for NLP systems and model design

Embeddings changed the design of neural language models and architectures by shifting NLP from sparse, high-dimensional representations to dense, lower-dimensional distributed representations [N4-F4]. This shift enabled more compact and meaningful representations than one-hot encoding, which uses isolated binary identifiers and lacks semantic structure [N4-F4]. The evidence also shows that embeddings paved the way for transfer learning and pre-training approaches. The MDPI paper on word embeddings and pre-trained language models explicitly frames embeddings as a foundation for later breakthroughs in pre-trained language models [N6-R3]. The evidence on contextualized embeddings, such as those from ELMo, shows that deeper models can encode meaning in hidden layers and produce word representations that incorporate context, which is a direct step toward transfer learning and pre-training [N6-R5].

### 6) Trade-offs that remain even with modern embeddings

Even with modern embeddings, trade-offs remain. The distributed-representations article notes that these representations require large amounts of data to learn meaningful relationships and can be computationally expensive [N4-F4]. It also says that distributed representations may lack interpretability because the dimensions do not correspond to easily understood features [N4-F4]. The word-embeddings overview likewise mentions that static embeddings conflate polysemous words into a single vector, and that multi-sense embeddings are needed to handle multiple meanings [N3-F3]. So while embeddings greatly improved modeling, they still require careful design, data, and interpretation to balance performance with computational and semantic limitations [N4-F4][N3-F3].

## Conclusion

Overall, word embedding techniques address the shortcomings of earlier high-dimensional semantic representations by replacing sparse, symbolic, and meaningless encodings with dense, continuous distributed representations. They capture semantic similarity and analogy through vector space proximity and arithmetic, capture context through co-occurrence and training objectives, and improve downstream NLP tasks by providing more compact and meaningful representations [N4-F4][N3-F3][N6-R2][N5-R3]. They also changed NLP systems and model design by enabling denser architectures, transfer learning, and pre-training, while still facing trade-offs related to data, computation, interpretability, and polysemy [N4-F4][N6-R3][N6-R5][N3-F3]. In short, embeddings moved NLP from shallow, high-dimensional representations to rich, context-aware semantic models that are much more effective for language understanding and downstream tasks.
